hypothesis: If Darwin's claim holds, no frog, toad or newt species is native to any truly oceanic island (volcanic or coral, never connected to a continent), whereas frogs introduced there by people have established populations.
pass_criterion: Across a pre-specified list of at least 30 oceanic islands or island groups, at most 1 (<=3%) has a native, non-introduced Anura or Caudata species recorded in AmphibiaWeb. The list is fixed before data are examined and uses the standard geological definition of oceanic: Hawaii, Azores, Madeira, Cape Verde, Galapagos, Ascension, St Helena, Tristan da Cunha, Bermuda, Mascarenes, Chagos, Marquesas, Society Islands, Samoa, Tonga, Fiji, Palau, Marianas, Sao Tome, Principe and similar. In addition, at least 3 of these islands must have established introduced frog populations, supporting the 'not unsuitable conditions' part of the claim.
fail_criterion: Two or more islands or island groups on the pre-specified oceanic list (more than 3% of the list) have at least one native frog, toad or newt species. Examples that would count include endemic Hyperolius or Phrynobatrachus on Sao Tome and Principe, and Cornufer/Platymantis on Fiji or Palau, unless geological evidence shows that island was once joined to a continent. Alternatively, fewer than 3 oceanic islands have established introduced frogs.
interpretation: 'Batrachians (frogs, toads, newts)' maps to the amphibian orders Anura and Caudata. Caecilians (Gymnophiona) are excluded, as Darwin did not include them. 'Oceanic islands' maps to the modern geological definition: islands of volcanic or coral origin never connected to a continent. Continental-shelf islands and continental fragments such as Madagascar, the Seychelles granitic islands, New Zealand, Japan and Britain are excluded. 'Naturally absent' maps to no native or endemic species in the country or island distribution fields. Introduced populations are identified from the notes on introduced ranges. The causal part of the claim, that sea-water kills the animals and their spawn, cannot be tested with this dataset. Only the distributional generalization and the introduction-success observation are tested. Darwin said he found it 'strictly true', so a single well-supported native counterexample on a genuinely oceanic island refutes the strict form. The pass threshold of at most 1 exception allows for classification disputes.

dataset.name: AmphibiaWeb
dataset.why_it_fits: AmphibiaWeb covers all described amphibian species. For each it gives order, taxonomy, country and distribution, and often a note on introduced ranges. The fields used would be order (Anura or Caudata), species, country or distribution, and the notes on introduced populations. These would be cross-referenced against the fixed oceanic-island list to count native versus introduced frogs. I have not checked whether the site offers bulk download or an API, so access is marked unknown.
